short.en: Min becomes sum, add becomes multiply

t.en: A different question: not “which tagging is best”, but “counting every tagging, how likely is this sentence to appear”.

Costs become probabilities (numbers between 0 and 1): the probability of one tagging is every probability along the way multiplied together; the probability of the sentence is all the taggings added up. “Start” holds 1.

Compare with <level-ref to="tagging"></level-ref>: there you wanted only the best tagging; here every tagging counts, and the parts of a tagging are multiplied this time. Which components in the circuit need swapping? When counting routes, you added up every route.
The little bar under a cell shows its share of its column: the longer the bar, the more likely this word is to be this part of speech.

goal.en: Work out how likely the sentence is: the sum of the probabilities of every tagging. Each tagging’s probability is the “after …” and “this word, this tag” probabilities along the way, multiplied together.

how.en: The circuit’s skeleton is the same as <level-ref to="tagging"></level-ref>’s: think about which components need swapping.

body.en: Same table, same skeleton: Viterbi is “min and add”, this is “sum and multiply”. The first finds the best tagging; the second counts them all.
This is the forward algorithm. When speech recognition compares “which sentence does this sound most resemble”, this is how it works out the probability of each sentence.

note.en: Forward algorithm: Viterbi’s “min and add” becomes “sum and multiply”.

say.en: This time you don’t pick the best one: every tagging counts, so use “sum”.

hints.en: Start from <level-ref to="tagging"></level-ref>’s circuit: which component joins the parts of one tagging, and which one chooses among the possibilities?
Add the three together, then multiply by the “this word, this tag” probability.
